presentingComplaint: Three-week history of daily throbbing holocranial headache with transient visual obscurations, worse on lying flat and on straining.
history: 34-year-old woman with known compensated autoimmune cirrhosis (on azathioprine and low-dose prednisolone) presents with a progressive 3-week history of daily, throbbing headache that is worse in the morning, on lying flat, and on coughing or bending. She reports brief episodes of greying-out of vision in both eyes lasting seconds, especially on standing, and horizontal double vision for the past week. She has pulsatile tinnitus (a 'whooshing' in both ears). She has gained ~9 kg over the last year (BMI 34). She denies fever, neck stiffness, seizures, limb weakness or altered behaviour. No recent tetracycline, retinoid or vitamin A use. Her cirrhosis has been stable with no prior encephalopathy; she has mild ascites managed with spironolactone. The overlap of headache, visual symptoms and background liver disease initially raised concern for hepatic encephalopathy or a hepatic-related metabolic disturbance, but she is fully alert and oriented with no asterixis.
examination: Alert, fully oriented, GCS 15. Obese (BMI 34). No asterixis, no jaundice of note, spider naevi and mild non-tense ascites consistent with known cirrhosis. Neurological exam: fundoscopy shows bilateral Frisen grade 3 papilloedema with blurred disc margins and obscuration of vessels. Visual acuity preserved but enlarged blind spots on confrontation; mild bilateral abducens (VI nerve) palsy causing horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze (false-localising sign). No other focal deficit, no neck stiffness, normal higher functions, gait and coordination.
imaging: MRI brain with contrast: no mass lesion, no hydrocephalus; normal ventricles, partially empty sella, flattening of the posterior globes and distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space. MR venography: patent dural venous sinuses with no thrombosis. These features support raised intracranial pressure without an obstructive or venous cause.
microbiology: Not applicable - CSF sterile with normal cell count, protein and glucose; no infective process identified.
differentialDiagnoses: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (confirmed by modified Dandy / Friedman criteria)
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (excluded on MR venography)
Space-occupying mass lesion / raised ICP from tumour
Hepatic encephalopathy (excluded - alert, no asterixis, normal ammonia, normal CSF)
finalDiagnosis: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumour cerebri) in a patient with background autoimmune cirrhosis; diagnosis by Friedman criteria - papilloedema, normal neuroimaging bar signs of raised ICP, normal CSF composition, and elevated CSF opening pressure (34 cmH2O).
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension / Pseudotumour Cerebri
American Academy of Neurology - Revised diagnostic criteria for pseudotumour cerebri syndrome (Friedman), 2013
stewardship: Non-infective condition - no antimicrobial therapy indicated. CSF sterility and normal composition exclude meningitis; antibiotics are not warranted.
contraindications: Acetazolamide should be used cautiously in hepatic impairment/cirrhosis - carbonic anhydrase inhibition can precipitate metabolic acidosis and hepatic encephalopathy, and cause hypokalaemia
Topiramate (alternative weight-neutral agent) also requires caution and dose consideration in hepatic/renal impairment
Avoid volume depletion and hypokalaemia in a cirrhotic on diuretics, which can precipitate encephalopathy
Avoid causative agents where relevant (tetracyclines, high-dose vitamin A, retinoids)
edgeCases: Fulminant IIH with rapidly progressive visual field loss - urgent CSF diversion (VP/LP shunt) or optic nerve sheath fenestration required
IIH in pregnancy - management differs, acetazolamide relative caution in first trimester
Secondary intracranial hypertension from drugs (tetracyclines, retinoids, vitamin A) - must be excluded before labelling idiopathic
Cirrhosis-related coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia increasing bleeding risk at lumbar puncture - check platelets/INR before LP
expectedMaiK: Confirm raised ICP with normal CSF and neuroimaging (Friedman criteria), protect vision with serial formal visual fields/OCT, initiate acetazolamide with caution given hepatic impairment (monitor for acidosis/encephalopathy and electrolytes), pursue weight management, and refer urgently for surgical CSF diversion if vision deteriorates.
expectedNextQuestions: Any pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations or diplopia?
Any use of tetracyclines, retinoids, high-dose vitamin A or recent weight gain?
Any features of hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, sleep reversal, precipitants) to exclude the cirrhosis-related mimic?
Formal visual acuity and perimetry - any field loss or reduced acuity threatening sight?

Lumbar puncture with measurement of CSF opening pressure and full CSF analysis

Baseline coagulation and platelets prior to LP given cirrhosis
